Intel wasn't trying nearly hard enough to bring mHz down. Which is why AMD ultimately came up with better solutions than Intel for both 64 bit and multiple cores.

A period of time in the late 90's when AMD and Intel were engaged in a pattern of one-upping to bring the fastest processor to market.

It ended when AMD went 64 bit, and then shortly thereafter cpus started to go multi-core.

This is a misunderstanding, we can make 9+Ghz cores no problem. Issue with higher clock speeds is that you end up having to push way more current through the cpu, this in turn creates more heat and resistance in the system so you have to push even more current. Its a land of diminishing returns, you can find people pushing over 7Ghz on a single P4 core with liquid or cryo cooling.

The magic is to use your Ghz more intelligently than your competitor and lower your power consumption if you want that laptop or smart device to A. not get really hot B. have a battery life worth speaking of. This is why intel never captured the smart device market, their designs had always involved ready access to large quantities of electricity, so their design ethos since the 60's was fundamentally incompatible with the new market space when it first emerged.

There's clock speed and there's throughput.

Intel was fixated on higher clock speeds at one time, hence the Mhz and Ghz wars. Like the other guy said, higher clock speed leads to all kinds of interesting problems in thermal dissipation. At those speeds, wires on the chip behave like waveguides.

To increase throughput, you need to do more every clock signal. If you look at RISC designs, they try to execute one instruction per cycle. Pipelining allows you to execute more than one instruction per cycle if you can keep the pipeline full.

Tricks like branch prediction and speculative execution were invented to keep the pipeline full.

It appears that these bugs rely on breaking those implicit assumptions.
